📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • They write, summarize, translate, and call tools.
  • According to recent reports, say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

According to recent reports, say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Sources indicate that computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's fresh speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

In a recent development, it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

It has been revealed that the package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

In a recent development, the steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

According to recent reports, parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Industry observers note that parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Sources indicate that qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

In a recent development, qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Industry observers note that each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Industry observers note that downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

Sources indicate that the diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

Recent findings suggest that anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't newly introduced, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

Sources indicate that if you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

It has been revealed that reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

Sources indicate that you use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Sources indicate that language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

In a recent development, like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Recent findings suggest that both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

In a recent development, try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#34097. The RegTech adoption divide: what solutions are proving popular?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2620 w)

The RegTech adoption divide: what solutions are proving popular?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fintech

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that regTech has quickly grown into a booming market, with use cases across all areas of compliance.
  • Industry observers note that regTech Analyst and Parker & Lawrence Research recently released a major industry report looking at the global state of RegTech in 2026.
  • To get some thoughts as to why some areas are seeing greater adoption, FinTech Global recently sat down with several leading players in RegTech to get their thoughts on why financial crime solutions are seeing the greatest level of adoption in the sector.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that regTech has quickly grown into a booming market, with use cases across all areas of compliance. While solutions of all types are being adopted, some areas are seeing a much greater level of deployment.

Industry observers note that regTech Analyst and Parker & Lawrence Research recently released a major industry report looking at the global state of RegTech in 2026. Among its findings, the report noted that financial crime solutions have the highest rate of adoption within compliance, but why is that the case?

To get some thoughts as to why some areas are seeing greater adoption, FinTech Global recently sat down with several leading players in RegTech to get their thoughts on why financial crime solutions are seeing the greatest level of adoption in the sector.

According to recent reports, as part of the report, which can be downloaded here, it set out to build greater structure to the fragmented market. It introduced a simplified RegTech taxonomy that covers 24 subcategories across six major risk and compliance domains. Using this framework, the report established a RegTech Adoption Index to measure relative maturity across the sector.

At the top of that list was financial crime, boasting an Index score of 68. This domain includes solutions that are designed to detect, prevent and respond to crimes impacting financial institutions, such as fraud, money laundering, sanctions evasion and terrorist financing.

Recent findings suggest that subsectors in this domain include sanctions screening, KYC/KYB, fraud prevention/FRAML, and transaction monitoring. The leading adopters of this technology are payment firms and investment banks.

Financial crime solutions lead the way.

There are a number of reasons that could explain why financial crime solutions have seen the greatest adoption within compliance.

For Chaitanya Sarda, CEO at AiPrise, it is because it is the only domain where all three conditions for adoption are present at once.

Recent findings suggest that sarda said, “There’s a named obligation with a deadline. There’s a measurable cost of failure, in fines and enforcement actions that appear in public. And there’s a testable output, since you can check whether a screening decision was right.”.

It has been revealed that this reason also explains other domains with high adoption, such as Information and Technology Security, which has the second highest Index score of 61. This is a space where failure is immediate, visible and priced.

In a similar vein, Nir Carciente, head of RegTech at ACA, also emphasised how financial crime’s dominance in RegTech adoption comes down to the high regulatory exposure. He noted that AML, KYC, sanctions and transaction monitoring combine high regulatory exposure with huge volumes of data and processes that are difficult to scale exclusively through people.

The financial damages from a financial crime failure are also growing, making poor financial crime processes a major risk to a financial institution. On top of this, the cost of operations within managing financial crime requirements are also increasing rapidly, especially for firms operating across multiple jurisdictions.

A 2024 report from BioCatch claimed that 58% of organisations said they spent between $5m and $25m in operational costs related to investigating, combating and rectifying financial crime issues in 2023.

Sources indicate that another reason why Carciente believes the financial crime domain has seen strong adoption comes to the fact the business case is easy to demonstrate. He mentioned, “Firms can measure alert volumes, false positives, investigation times and manual review effort. When technology improves those metrics, the impact is visible.

Sources indicate that “That hasn’t always been true elsewhere in compliance. Regulatory pressure by itself doesn’t guarantee technology adoption. In my experience, adoption moves fastest when the risk is material, the existing process doesn’t scale and there is a measurable benefit from changing it. Financial crime reached that point earlier than most other compliance disciplines.”.

Recent findings suggest that relyComply noted that the adoption of RegTech within financial crime is a response to the growing sophistication coming from the criminal underworld. “From exploiting the rise of digital assets, to employing crypto scams and using dark-web identity marketplaces to commit synthetic identity fraud, the underbelly is looking bleaker by the day.

“Add on the fact that regulatory concerns are created in response to this activity, it is perhaps unsurprising (and welcome) that retail and investment banks, payments firms and FinTechs are treating areas such as money laundering and terrorist financing with greater importance. Each form of crime puts their customers at risk – so too their regulatory reputations, where failing anti-fincrime controls could cause irreparable damage.”.

Sources indicate that at the other end of the adoption index is the ESG domain, which has the lowest index score of 40. This domain covers solutions facilitating the measurement, management and reporting of environmental, social and governance factors for sustainable investing and corporate responsibility. Subcategories in this domain include ESG ratings, ESG reporting and disclosures, ESG risk management and climate risk quantification.

In a recent development, the Compliance Management domain has the second lowest adoption in compliance, with an Index score of 44. This domain refers to solutions helping to address regulatory challenges across multiple domains and frameworks. These are tools that help proactively manage regulatory obligations, changes and assurance activities across the enterprise. Subcategories include regulatory change management, regulatory intelligence, compliance assessment and compliance orchestration.

Much like how Sarda believes financial crime has led the charge with adoption due to the immediate and visible failures, compliance management and ESG lack this. Sarda said, “The obligations are broad rather than specific, failure is diffuse and slow to surface, and there’s no clean way to demonstrate the tool worked. That isn’t a reflection of the software. It’s a reflection of what firms can justify spending on.”.

In a recent development, another reason why financial crime solutions have been popular could be down to the age of obligation. Copla CEO Aurimas Bakas stated, “Adoption tracks the age of the obligation and how clearly it names someone accountable. Financial crime has decades of prescriptive rules behind it, a public enforcement record with named penalties, and in the UK a statutory owner in the MLRO.

In a recent development, “A vendor market has had time to mature against requirements that hold still. Information and technology security at 61 follows the same pattern, with data protection law, established security standards and a long incident history to build against.”.

As such, the domains that are newly introduced obligations have lower adoption scores, Bakas stated. For instance, the Resilience domain has an Index score of 46. The Resilience category covers solutions that ensure the continuity of critical business services by enabling firms to prepare for, respond to and recover from disruptions across operational and third-party environments. It includes the subcategories AI governance, third-party risk, incident response and enterprise risk management.

In a recent development, third party risk only became a live submission requirement in the EU through the recently deployed DORA that requires the register of information. Similarly, the UK equivalent for material third-party arrangements is only coming through with PS26/2. AI governance is even newer.

Sources indicate that the leading adopters for resilience are retail banks and investment banks, which Bakas noted are the institutions under the closest supervision. “When we speak to firms, movement on third party risk tends to begin with a supervisory conversation or a correction on a submitted register. Adoption there is following supervisory pressure, and the score reflects how recently that pressure arrived.”.

Why is there still relatively modest adoption.

According to recent reports, the RegTech sector is no longer a niche market. The global RegTech market size is estimated to be worth $29.3bn in 2026. It is also projected to grow rapidly and become valued at $112.1bn by 2033. Despite the size of the market, the scores on the adoption index suggest the adoption of RegTech solutions is still rather modest across financial services.

Bakas noted that the modest nature of adoption is simply because the tools are coming quicker to the market than the regulations are. He stated, “Investment into the sector is running ahead of the obligations that pull tools into production. Firms commit when a requirement has a deadline, a named owner and a defined data format. Several categories in this taxonomy have the first two and are still waiting on the third.”.

It has been revealed that sarda noted that the adoption index does not necessarily suggest that financial institutions are not working with tools in these domains. The index score captures the depth of the adoption, and not whether the firm has bought a solution. Most of the firm, Sarda explained, have bought something in each of the six RegTech domains highlighted in the report. However, they are not running them independently.

In a recent development, “What they haven’t done is let it run the process unsupervised. Adoption stalls at parallel running, where the tool is live but a person still owns every decision, and it stays there until the buyer can defend the output to a regulator. Twenty years of AML enforcement has produced a score of 68 in the most mature domain. That tells you how slowly the ceiling moves in supervised environments.”.

The modest adoption is not a result of a shortage of technology, Carciente stated. Instead, the challenge is the environment the technology needs to adapt to. Most large financial institutions have built their systems over decades, with newly introduced tools slowly embraced, typically in isolation. One team handles employee compliance, another does communications surveillance, another manages trade surveillance, etc.

Adding to the complexity is the various types of tools, whether it is an internal application, outsourced process or manual workflow.

“Individually, these systems may work well. The difficulty comes when firms try to connect them.

“Data is fragmented, context gets lost between systems and integrations become expensive to maintain. We increasingly hear firms questioning whether they need another point solution or whether they need to simplify and connect what they already have.”.

Recent findings suggest that this is unfortunately changing the RegTech adoption conversation. Instead of being whether the tool can solve a compliance problem, it is more focused on whether it can fit into the overall compliance operating model.

“I think that shift will shape the next three to five years. AI will accelerate it, but it won’t remove accountability.”.

Despite there being modest adoption within RegTech, RelyComply emphasised there is more that needs to be done. There are still major institutions failing to file timely reports, conduct continuous monitoring or handle risk-based onboarding.

RelyComply sees two areas need to change to support greater adoption of RegTech solutions.

Industry observers note that they said, “Fixing the lack of internal human skill and ownership culture, for one. The second is more material: addressing budget concerns under the dreaded ‘cost of compliance’ alongside legacy technology that’s causing disparate data, and AML and fraud workflows before any real-time systems can be integrated.”.

One challenge RelyComply pointed out was the need for a breakdown of silos.

Firms need to ensure there is some level of governance to ensure tools don’t overlap and cause confusion across compliance teams. While teams might look to certain RegTech tools that can solve unique solutions, they need to ensure ownership does not become blurred.

RelyComply stated that if one reporting engine is selected and another generative AI tool is used to collate auto-fill suspicious activity reports, it is bound to create mix-ups around who is responsible for overseeing the processes, utilising the same quality data as a different member that is tracking a different active investigation.

According to recent reports, “AI-based platforms may feel like a band-aid to automate everything. Yet there is no guarantee multiple tools can be engineered to suit a one-view AML, fraud and risk effort at all. Not to mention a stifled skills gap when AI implementations (handled in-house or through third parties) require not just advanced expertise, but a documented plan for how AI models can be audited by an institution’s compliance teams.”.

Where will adoption grow the fastest?

The areas that will see the greatest adoption over the coming years is open for debate. AiPrise’s Sarda believes the mandates will be the defining factor behind which domains see the most adoption, rather than enthusiasm for the tools.

It has been revealed that with that in mind, Sarda expects the Resilience domain will have a greater adoption Index score in the next five years, largely due to the AI governance space growing. The EU AI Act, for instance, will help to give the space a named obligation and deadline to adhere to, and other countries around the world are all set for similar rules around AI in the coming years.

Sources indicate that bakas also considered resilience as one of the domains that will see greater adoption levels in the coming years. He mentioned, “In the EU, DORA made the register of information an annual submission with a defined data model, and the first cycle produced corrections that showed firms precisely where their data was weak. In the UK, PS26/2 brings reporting of material third party arrangements into scope, which gives firms a format to build toward.”.

In a similar vein, Carciente also pointed to the rising prominence of AI governance also increasing the adoption of resilience solutions in the coming years. As AI models become more integral to the running of business services, whether from internal models or the third-party dependence, they pose a major risk for firms.

Industry observers note that “As financial institutions deploy more AI, they need to know where it is being used, what data it accesses, what decisions it influences and what controls and oversight are required. AI won’t just change RegTech; it creates a newly introduced category of risk that firms need to govern.”.

Carciente pointed to a couple of other domains that could see strong adoption in the next few years. Surveillance tools are prime for this adoption growth. Carciente explained that firms must now monitor risk through email, messaging, voice, mobile communications and trading activity. This is becoming unsustainable through manual workloads and AI is helping to reduce noise and identify across the various datasets rather than creating false alerts or missing signals.

It has been revealed that carciente also sees regulatory change management generating a lot of adoption in the coming years, spurred on by the increased pace of change. There is an unprecedented level of regulatory change and firms have to monitor multiple updates and changes each week, not only understanding the changes but whether they are affected and what measures they need to take.

The underlying theme of RegTech adoption in the coming years, Carciente noted, will be the shift from disconnected applications towards more integrated compliance environments.

“The first phase of RegTech largely digitized individual compliance processes. The next phase will be about connecting them: common data, connected workflows, case management, evidence and AI working across that information without losing context.”.

It has been revealed that “Ultimately, financial crime’s lead isn’t an anomaly. It shows what happens when regulatory risk, operational scale and measurable value come together. Other areas of compliance are now reaching similar pressure points. Teams are managing more data, more channels, more regulatory change and now more AI, often without significantly more resources.

Recent findings suggest that “For me, that is where the next stage of RegTech becomes interesting. It won’t simply be about adding more automation or more tools. It will be about connecting data and workflows and using AI within a framework that firms can govern and defend. Financial crime demonstrated how technology can fundamentally change a compliance function. The opportunity now is to apply those lessons more broadly.”.

AWS Network Firewall introduces automated Internet firewall (Preview)

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AWS Network Firewall introduces the public preview of automated internet firewall (Preview), a latest centralized control that allows you to configure Network Firewall, with native network address translation (NAT) capability, on the internet gateways of all the Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) in your environment.
  • Recent findings suggest that AWS Network Firewall is a stateful, managed, network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service for your VPC.
  • To help you get started promptly, automated internet firewall comes with a default security policy, which uses Amazon managed rule groups including active threat defense that uses AWS unique threat intelligence to protect your workloads against evolving threats on the internet.

According to recent reports, AWS Network Firewall introduces the public preview of automated internet firewall (Preview), a latest centralized control that allows you to configure Network Firewall, with native network address translation (NAT) capability, on the internet gateways of all the Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) in your environment. Using automated internet firewall (Preview) mode, you can centrally define your Network Firewall security rules and enforce them on all inbound and outbound traffic across the internet gateways of your VPCs. You are not required to make routing or architectural changes to deploy automated internet firewall (Preview). You can deploy it across select VPCs or your entire account, organization or organization unit.

Recent findings suggest that AWS Network Firewall is a stateful, managed, network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service for your VPC. Customers use it to inspect their traffic and secure AWS resources. Prior to this launch, customers would configure AWS Network Firewalls inside their VPCs in the traffic path of all internet communication to achieve thorough security coverage against the threats on the internet. They deployed Network Firewall endpoints in dedicated subnets and made route updates for every subnet that needed internet access across all their VPCs. In addition, they monitored the environment to ensure that no upcoming internet network paths bypassed these security controls. Automated internet firewall (Preview) makes this deployment and management simpler. You just define and maintain filtering rules, and AWS enforces it directly at the internet gateway of every VPC in scope, ensuring that all intended traffic entering or leaving your VPCs via the internet gateway is inspected. Automated Internet firewall comes with built-in NAT functionality for your egress-only internet connectivity needs. You can use it to filter traffic, perform NAT and log all internet activity across all internet gateways. You don't need to make architectural changes inside every VPC or monitor every internet network path. Automated Internet firewall (Preview) allows you the option to automatically extend your organization's security policy to all future VPCs and subnets at creation.

To help you get started promptly, automated internet firewall comes with a default security policy, which uses Amazon managed rule groups including active threat defense that uses AWS unique threat intelligence to protect your workloads against evolving threats on the internet. You can also create your own custom rule groups or use any of the managed rule groups from AWS Marketplace with automated internet firewall.

AWS Network Firewall operating in automated internet firewall mode (Preview) is available in preview in all AWS Regions except MXP, AWS GovCloud, and China. To learn more, visit the Network Firewall documentation and see the AWS Network Firewall pricing page. To get started, visit the Amazon VPC or Network Security Manager console.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Sources indicate that mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That stated, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

It has been revealed that for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

Industry observers note that on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

In a recent development, cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

According to recent reports, the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AWS Lambda now publishes Event Function state change events to Amazon EventBridge.
  • Customers use Lambda Event Functions to build APIs, event processing workloads, multi-step workflows, and data pipelines.
  • It has been revealed that this feature is available in all commercial AWS Regions.

It has been revealed that AWS Lambda now publishes Event Function state change events to Amazon EventBridge. Lambda emits an event each time an Event Function version changes state because of a customer action, such as creating, updating, publishing, or deleting a function. These events help platform and DevOps teams to trigger automation as soon as a function becomes ready to invoke, an update finishes, or an operation fails, without polling the GetFunction API.

Customers use Lambda Event Functions to build APIs, event processing workloads, multi-step workflows, and data pipelines. As organizations grow to thousands of functions, platform teams need to know when a function changes state so they can take the next step. For example, a deployment pipeline can run integration tests and then shift alias traffic once a new version becomes active. Until now, these tools had to poll the GetFunction API to track state changes. Polling consumed API quota, slowed down pipelines, and required custom retry logic, which added operational overhead. With this launch, you can create EventBridge rules that match on fields such as the function ARN, detail type, or state, and route matched events to targets such as AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS, or Amazon SQS. This helps you build reliable, event-driven deployment pipelines across all of your functions, without writing or maintaining custom polling logic.

It has been revealed that this feature is available in all commercial AWS Regions. You can create rules by using the EventBridge console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), or AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM). Lambda publishes these events automatically at no additional cost. Standard pricing applies to the targets that your EventBridge rules invoke. To learn more, see the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and the Amazon EventBridge User Guide.

  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Recent findings suggest that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to strategy for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

Industry observers note that but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

In a recent development, project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

Recent findings suggest that the pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

In a recent development, figure 1. Upcoming public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

Industry observers note that when organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Recent findings suggest that publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

Recent findings suggest that this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

It has been revealed that making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an vital first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

Recent findings suggest that to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

In a recent development, the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

In a recent development, participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

It has been revealed that beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be unveiled through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

It has been revealed that we also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

It has been revealed that amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now provides a Primary Endpoint, a DNS name that always resolves to the current primary DB instance in a replica configuration. When you switch over to an Oracle replica, Amazon RDS points the Primary Endpoint to the new primary DB instance, so you don't need to change your application connection strings. Previously, after each switchover, you had to update connection strings or DNS records to point to the new primary DB instance, which often required change approvals and coordination across teams.

With Primary Endpoint, you can run planned switchovers, such as disaster recovery drills, to replicas in the same AWS Region or to cross-Region replicas without changing your application configuration. If your applications connect through the Primary Endpoint, you don't need to enhancement their connection strings after the switchover.

Every RDS for Oracle Enterprise Edition DB instance has a Primary Endpoint at no additional charge, and you don't have to create it. The Primary Endpoint is provided in addition to the instance endpoint, so your existing applications aren't affected.

Primary Endpoint is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Oracle is available. To learn more, see Using the Primary Endpoint for Amazon RDS for Oracle in the Amazon RDS User Guide.

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding newly introduced expertise on a single endpoint.

It has been revealed that granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these upcoming features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

Flows in AWS Quick now lets users build, run, and refine automations for themselves and their teams, all through conversation. Users describe a process in chat, and Quick builds the flow, with no coding needed.

Flows can now orchestrate agents, skills, and tools, with access to structured data, knowledge, and apps. A flow can pull answers from the business data a team already reports on, produce ready-to-share documents, spreadsheets, and presentations, and save the results to a team space. Flows also support longer-running workflows and larger volumes of data.

In a recent development, fresh deterministic steps help keep results consistent, and validations check each step's output against rules the user sets, such as requiring a summary table in a report, before the flow continues. For example, an accounts payable team can build a flow that uses agents to read invoices and match them to purchase orders, and deterministic steps to check totals and catch duplicates.

Sources indicate that owners can now run flows wherever they work, across desktop, web, and mobile. In the desktop app, flows can work with local files and complete tasks in the browser. In the mobile app, users can start flows and check on them on the go.

These updates are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Quick is available.

To learn more, see Flows in AWS Quick in the AWS Quick User Guide and the AWS Quick product page.

Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • According to recent reports, when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • In a recent development, transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is substantial: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

According to recent reports, when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

In a recent development, transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is substantial: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Sources indicate that our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Industry observers note that model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

It has been revealed that A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

According to recent reports, for example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

Sources indicate that A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

It has been revealed that we also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

Recent findings suggest that the Llama 4 Scout shrink report indicates what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

It has been revealed that our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a latest model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a upcoming model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

Sources indicate that so we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

Recent findings suggest that the Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

It has been revealed that as of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

Web Search on Amazon Bedrock, the tool that grounds AI agents and applications in cited, current web information, now supports five newly introduced languages, plus non-US English, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock: Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Japanese. Agents serving customers in these languages get results that draw on local-language sources.

Industry observers note that we are also introducing a latest optional country field that biases results toward sources from a specific country - just pass an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code, such as “JP” or “DE”. This is useful for agents that serve users in multiple countries, for questions whose answer depends on the user's actual or preferred location (e.g., local regulations, prices or public officials), and for surfacing regional sources.

Both the expanded language support and the optional  country field are available today in every Region where Web Search is offered: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland) for Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and US Regions for Web Search on Amazon Bedrock. Queries are processed in the Region you call, helping organizations meet data residency requirements. Existing customers get the new language capabilities automatically, with no code changes, and pricing is the same in every language.

To get started with Web Search on Amazon Bedrock, checkout the developer guide and the web search product page.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

It has been revealed that our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

It has been revealed that results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where fresh models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

It has been revealed that of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

It has been revealed that -k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.
