💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML now lets customers search across multiple instance types and AWS Regions in a single search, making it easier to find and reserve the capacity their ML workloads need.
  • Industry observers note that until now, customers looking to buy Capacity Blocks had to run a separate search for every instance type and Region combination.
  • This feature is available for all Instance Capacity Blocks in AWS Regions where EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML are offered.

Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML now lets customers search across multiple instance types and AWS Regions in a single search, making it easier to find and reserve the capacity their ML workloads need. With Capacity Blocks for ML, customers can reserve accelerated compute instances such as Amazon EC2 P6-B300, P6-B200, and Trn2 instances, for a future start date and for up to 6 months.

Industry observers note that until now, customers looking to buy Capacity Blocks had to run a separate search for every instance type and Region combination. Starting today, customers can use a single search in the AWS Management Console to look for Capacity Blocks across multiple instance types and Regions, making it easier to secure capacity without repeated searches. Customers can also programmatically search for capacity across multiple instance types within a Region with a single API call using DescribeCapacityBlockOfferings.

This feature is available for all Instance Capacity Blocks in AWS Regions where EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML are offered. For a complete list of supported regions, refer to Capacity Blocks documentation. To get started, visit the Capacity Blocks page in the Amazon EC2 console.

Industry News: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time.
  • It has been revealed that tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment.
  • According to recent reports, building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.

It has been revealed that tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4).

According to recent reports, building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps customers entirely in control of their digital lives.

BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

Learning from demonstrations (SFT).

According to recent reports, we first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages).

Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

It has been revealed that the second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

Recent findings suggest that botPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

In a recent development, table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Industry observers note that table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

It has been revealed that botPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

It has been revealed that table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

According to recent reports, the largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

Sources indicate that botPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Sources indicate that complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

In a recent development, botPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

According to recent reports, shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):.

In a recent development, it does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

According to recent reports, botPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

In a recent development, botPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AWS Systems Manager Automation now lets you create custom workflows (runbooks) that can automate operational tasks across Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and AWS resources.
  • Six new runbook actions call Azure and Google Cloud APIs, check a resource's state, and wait for operations to finish without custom code.
  • This capability is available in all AWS Regions where you can create a Systems Manager Cloud Connector.

Sources indicate that AWS Systems Manager Automation now lets you create custom workflows (runbooks) that can automate operational tasks across Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and AWS resources. Automation helps you make changes safely at scale, such as remediating misconfigurations or cleaning up idle resources. Runbooks can roll out in controlled batches, pause for approval, and stop if errors pass a threshold. Instead of maintaining separate tools and credentials for each cloud, teams can now author and execute runbooks from a single place.

Six new runbook actions call Azure and Google Cloud APIs, check a resource's state, and wait for operations to finish without custom code. You can target Azure resources by subscription, region, resource group, resource type, and tag. Google Cloud resources can be targeted by project, zone, asset type, and label. For more complex logic, aws:executeScript now includes Azure and Google Cloud Python SDKs and gets short-lived credentials from your Systems Manager Cloud Connector, so you don't store secrets in runbooks. For example, you can stop tagged development virtual machines outside business hours or fix storage buckets that don't meet your security policy. To get started, use the AWS-provided runbooks that install the SSM Agent or the Amazon Inspector agent on your Azure or Google Cloud virtual machines, or create your own custom workflow.

This capability is available in all AWS Regions where you can create a Systems Manager Cloud Connector. To learn more, see Run automations on multicloud resources in the AWS Systems Manager User Guide, or visit the AWS Systems Manager product page.

The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs.
  • 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment.
  • TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

In a recent development, the same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

It has been revealed that A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Industry observers note that our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

Recent findings suggest that loRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:.

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

Recent findings suggest that first, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid reveals if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

It has been revealed that O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

Recent findings suggest that in the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

In a recent development, we add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

It has been revealed that our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

It has been revealed that A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:.

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:.

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

In a recent development, the preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:.

This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

Sources indicate that if you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

Sources indicate that the commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:.

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso.

In a recent development, we use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object.

The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

In a recent development, we use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

According to recent reports, it’s notable to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We revision only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

We then follow these steps within the training loop:.

Sources indicate that the training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

Sources indicate that we trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:.

According to recent reports, in the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

According to recent reports, phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

According to recent reports, gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

It demonstrates how parameter-efficient training can make model customization more accessible without requiring the resources associated with full fine-tuning. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens.
  • Sources indicate that to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models.
  • Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

Sources indicate that to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

According to recent reports, JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

Recent findings suggest that LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):.

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

Industry observers note that the role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

Sources indicate that we compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

Recent findings suggest that in short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

Sources indicate that LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

That's really awesome! With an Apple pkl community renderer, you could potentially write PKL and render LLMON. 🥒🍋.

Any-to-pkl-community will convert json, yaml, toml to pkl, so just need the render part.

This is an interesting development, especially the idea of giving LLMs a more explicit structure for understanding instructions, data, and their relationships. The discussion about prompt injection and separating instructions from input data is particularly relevant as organizations build more advanced LLM applications. Implementing these approaches requires engineers who understand model behavior, fine-tuning, context management, and evaluation. I think these technical requirements are vital when estimating the cost to hire an LLM engineer, particularly for specialized enterprise projects. I came across this resource that explores the different factors involved: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/cost-to-hire-llm-engineer-2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Automated API discovery and protection are now generally available, enabling you to discover every API behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS Organization and protect them using AWS WAF.
  • Discovery is available through the fresh API Gateway API Portal, which identifies the APIs automatically from traffic logs and service configuration records, with no agents to deploy or logs to forward.
  • Industry observers note that protection is available through the new AWS WAF API Security managed rule group, which protects your APIs against the most exploited API attack categories: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA), where the attackers change record IDs in requests to read other customers' data, Broken Authentication and Credential Stuffing, where the attackers forge tokens or try stolen passwords at scale, and API Reconnaissance and Enumeration, where the attackers map an API by guessing hidden routes and probing for exposed docs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Automated API discovery and protection are now generally available, enabling you to discover every API behind Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon CloudFront across your AWS Organization and protect them using AWS WAF.

Discovery is available through the fresh API Gateway API Portal, which identifies the APIs automatically from traffic logs and service configuration records, with no agents to deploy or logs to forward. The API Portal classifies the APIs it finds, identifies zombie and shadow APIs, evaluates each API's security posture, and reports findings, including the ones that are missing WAF protections. For unprotected APIs, customers can enable protection using WAF.

Industry observers note that protection is available through the new AWS WAF API Security managed rule group, which protects your APIs against the most exploited API attack categories: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA), where the attackers change record IDs in requests to read other customers' data, Broken Authentication and Credential Stuffing, where the attackers forge tokens or try stolen passwords at scale, and API Reconnaissance and Enumeration, where the attackers map an API by guessing hidden routes and probing for exposed docs. The events detected by WAF are consolidated into the API Portal findings to provide a complete security picture of your APIs. You can use API Security alongside other AWS Managed Rules or your own custom rules to protect your applications.

Together, API Portal and API Security provide you a complete solution from discovery of all APIs in your AWS environment to protecting them, without having to write any custom rules.

Recent findings suggest that API Portal is available in 32 AWS Regions. See the Amazon API Gateway FAQ for the list. API Security is available in all AWS Regions where AWS WAF is available, except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

To get started, see the following resources:.

  • During the 3.5 years since its inception, the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

During the 3.5 years since its inception, the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work. We expect this trend to continue as local AI and privacy become increasingly important in our everyday lives. Every new integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount.

Recent findings suggest that today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:.

In a recent development, we are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-owners. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

According to recent reports, the project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

In a recent development, the underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the at the moment implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. At the moment, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's.
  • The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

According to recent reports, today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:.

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent.

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise prepares include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

Sources indicate that the best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million owners, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Industry observers note that before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:.

Sources indicate that routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Recent findings suggest that pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO owners get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

In a recent development, on model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics indicates the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:.

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:.

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:.

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

💡 Key Takeaways

  • audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.
  • It has been revealed that rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

It has been revealed that rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

Sources indicate that on-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

According to recent reports, on the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

In a recent development, rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Sources indicate that clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

Sources indicate that the weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

Sources indicate that we're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

Recent findings suggest that AWS CodeDeploy can now suspend Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes during EC2 in-place deployments to Auto Scaling groups. CodeDeploy is a fully managed service that automates application deployments to Amazon EC2 instances, on-premises servers, AWS Lambda functions, and Amazon ECS services. This launch helps prevent scaling activities from terminating or replacing instances while CodeDeploy is updating them, which can cause a deployment to fail.

Industry observers note that you can choose to suspend any combination of these processes (Terminate, AZRebalance, InstanceRefresh, and ScheduledActions) on a deployment group, or on a single deployment. CodeDeploy suspends the processes you choose before it deploys and resumes them when the deployment succeeds, fails, or is stopped, so you don't need custom scripts to suspend and resume processes during deployments. A setting on the deployment group applies to every deployment in that group, including deployments that your existing pipelines start.

You can configure this feature by using the CodeDeploy console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or AWS SDKs. This feature is available in all AWS Regions, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions.

To learn more, see Suspending Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes during deployments in the AWS CodeDeploy User Guide, or visit the AWS CodeDeploy product page.

#34056. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1844 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.
  • I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.
  • Recent findings suggest that orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Recent findings suggest that orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

Industry observers note that my first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Recent findings suggest that strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

Recent findings suggest that vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's significant batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Recent findings suggest that transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:.

It has been revealed that offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the massive model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

Recent findings suggest that the fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

According to recent reports, I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:.

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:.

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization strategy of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:.

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:.

Recent findings suggest that strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

Recent findings suggest that I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Industry observers note that most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:.

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:.

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:.

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Sources indicate that most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

According to recent reports, it runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Recent findings suggest that transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

In a recent development, beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

Sources indicate that the generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

  • With runtime reachability analysis, you can focus remediation efforts on vulnerabilities that matter most to your security posture.
  • Runtime reachability for Inspector findings is available at no additional charge and is available in all AWS Regions where Inspector is already available.

Amazon Inspector has expanded its vulnerability management capabilities with runtime reachability analysis for findings originating from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances. Previously, Inspector reported every vulnerability found in a resource, including packages that were never used by applications. Security teams had to manually assess which vulnerabilities actually posed risk in their deployed environments. Now, Inspector automatically identifies which vulnerabilities are potentially reachable by analyzing package placement in container images and process activity on EC2 instances.

With runtime reachability analysis, you can focus remediation efforts on vulnerabilities that matter most to your security posture. For container images, Inspector determines whether a vulnerable package is within your application's dockerfile paths defined by WORKDIR, ENTRYPOINT, or CMD instructions. For EC2 instances, Inspector identifies whether a vulnerable package was observed running as a process during the most recent scan. For EC2, customers must use the Inspector VM Scanner for agent-based scanning to get this capability. This helps organizations managing large container fleets or complex applications prioritize remediation by distinguishing between vulnerabilities that are potentially reachable versus those in unused dependencies, reducing noise and enabling development and security teams to work more efficiently. Newly generated findings will have runtime reachability analysis included, and backfill of existing findings will be completed over time.

Runtime reachability for Inspector findings is available at no additional charge and is available in all AWS Regions where Inspector is already available.

To learn more, visit the Amazon Inspector product page.
