How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust.
  • In a recent development, open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them.
  • The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.

In a recent development, open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.

According to recent reports, in the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.

In a recent development, AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software concerns and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.

Recent findings suggest that lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.

Sources indicate that figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.

In a recent development, we’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.

It has been revealed that figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.

There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.

It has been revealed that demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.

At the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis indicates 60% of its Intelligence Index v5, revealed in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations, where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable.

In a recent development, with the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation.

We work through eight steps: define the claim, find a task, run it unchanged, adapt it, check the evaluation, read the traces, report the score, and compare models. We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A. Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example.

Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel reveals what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results.

Claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

It has been revealed that starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no new work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A.

Adaptation. We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote newly introduced instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

According to recent reports, checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself.

In a recent development, shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it.

According to recent reports, figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut demonstrated that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model said it was done).

Recent findings suggest that baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

According to recent reports, traces and score. On the eight adapted tasks, we ran three rollouts per task. The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file. Several of these began with a script failing because NumPy or SciPy was missing, which the task expects the agent to install. Most failures therefore came from stopping early or from a missing package, and only two of the 13 failed the fit check (Figure 7 in Appendix A). Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time. Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more. The mean pass rate was 0.46, with a standard error of about 0.11 when rollouts are clustered by task. A repeat run passed 10 of 24. With eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to fresh spectra.

Model comparison. We then compared six models on the same eight tasks (Figure 4). Several providers can serve the same open-weight model with different quantization and context limits, so we pinned one provider per model. With DeepInfra pinned as the provider, gpt-oss-120b passed 13 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the earlier run, which used the default provider. Only gpt-oss-120b declared completion in its first response, in 22 of 24 rollouts. None of the other five models did so in any rollout (Figure 9 in Appendix A). The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

In a recent development, our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio without fitting a spectrum. A verifier that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks on all eight tasks. We found it by trying to break the grader with a solution we knew was incomplete, then added checks on the fitted spectrum (Appendix A, Step 5).

It has been revealed that the shortcut got the right answer for the wrong reason, like a student who copies the final number without the working. The lesson for us was to test what the output demonstrates. A faster valid method should pass; a method that skips a required skill should not. Domain experts can help set tolerances so the verifier accepts alternative correct fits without accepting work that misses the point of the task.

Sources indicate that such errors are common, and they move scores considerably. A review of agentic benchmarks found that flaws in task setup or reward design can shift measured performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

Public review can expose errors in instructions and tests that benchmark builders missed. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of its 89 tasks after user reports, including one whose tests expected Spark SQL while its instructions asked for PostgreSQL, and agent rankings stayed stable through the correction.

Access to the evidence also determines how much work an outside audit takes. CritPt keeps its reference solutions private, so the physicists who audited it had to solve the problems themselves before finding errors in 21 of the 56 challenges they reviewed. The authors then released a corrected version. OpenAI's audit of SWE-bench Verified found material challenges in 59.4% of the 138 problems it examined, working from tasks and tests that anyone can read. For a builder, outside scrutiny is part of validation: publish what reviewers need to challenge a task, give them a way to report problems, and record what changed.

According to recent reports, similar flaws emerged in SWE-bench Pro. In July 2026 OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks were broken and withdrew its recommendation to adopt it. Benchmark validation needs to continue after release.

In a recent development, A consistent score can still measure the wrong thing. Measuring what Matters, a review of 445 LLM benchmarks by 29 expert reviewers, found recurring patterns in tasks and metrics that undermine construct validity: whether the tasks and metrics support claims about the intended capability.

Industry observers note that for example, fitting synthetic spectra does not establish that an agent can review lab reports. That may also require recognizing a poor measurement or asking for help. If every task supplies a usable spectrum, the test cannot show whether the agent knows when a fit would be inappropriate.

Harder Than the Task extends this concern to organizational work, where authority, distributed knowledge, and dependencies can decide success. Its authors find that fewer than one quarter of prominent benchmarks claim to cover any such dimension. An agent may need calibration data from another team or permission to replace a measurement, and supplying everything at the outset removes those difficulties. If they matter to the claim, they belong in the evaluation. If they do not, it is enough to say that they remain untested.

Industry observers note that each error is worth a short record: the failed assumption, how it was found, and what changed. The record should also name the affected versions and say whether earlier scores remain comparable.

Industry observers note that the SWE-bench Verified audit described above also found contamination: every frontier model tested could reproduce the reference patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks. SWE-bench's public repositories and wide use exposed tasks to training. The openness that enabled scrutiny of bad tests also made items easier to encounter before evaluation.

Recent findings suggest that however, if contamination is carefully controlled for during training, hiding the test set by itself does not prevent saturation. A study of 60 language model benchmarks found similar saturation in public and private ones, and concluded that hiding test data does not prevent saturation once a benchmark is widely adopted, meaning a good benchmark falls out of use due to saturation without developers being able to learn from and build on it. What did correspond to lower saturation was expert curation and a larger test set.

This leaves a practical release question: what can we expose for review while protecting active test items?

Recent findings suggest that balancing contamination risks against saturation requires a strategic approach to what content is made public. Rather than treating openness as an all-or-nothing decision, benchmark creators can decide what to release part by part, protecting active test tasks from data leakage while still sharing the underlying infrastructure, grading methods, and reference examples that allow external researchers to audit and build upon the evaluation.

Existing benchmarks show a range of openness. ARC-AGI-2 publishes a training set and a 120-task evaluation set, and holds back semi-private and private sets of 120 tasks each. AILuminate keeps its official prompts confidential, publishes its methods and taxonomy, and keeps the underlying evidence for controlled review by authorized auditors and trusted researchers. Terminal-Bench publishes its tasks and marks their files with a canary string asking that they stay out of training corpora. No public reviewer can check a protected item, so whatever stays closed needs a review route of its own.

Table 1 outlines the core considerations of open sourcing an evaluation: what can be open, where it lives on the Hugging Face Hub, and what may stay protected. It has one row for each component in Figure 2, so you can go straight to the part you are about to release.

Table 1. What to open, how to share it on the Hugging Face Hub, and what can stay protected, for each evaluation component.

In a recent development, our own example follows this approach. We released raman-lab as a dataset on the Hub. It includes eight synthetic graphene spectra in Harbor task format, each with its environment, reference fit, verifier, and tolerances. The raw rollouts behind our results are shared as a separate dataset including Harbor trial folders with trajectories and verifier output for all six models. The spectrum generator, analysis code, and results are in a companion GitHub repository, so both the agent harness and the evaluation harness can be inspected and rerun.

In a recent development, in a more sensitive domain, a clinical evaluation could open its environment definition, harness, tool interfaces, and grading framework, with synthetic cases for development use. Patient records and reference answers would stay under controlled access while authorized reviewers inspect disputed judgments. Each restriction should come with a condition for revisiting it.

We recommend a short checklist, drawn in part from the more comprehensive Agentic Benchmark Checklist. Before releasing or retiring an evaluation, check that another builder can:.

These release decisions also determine what remains useful when the benchmark no longer separates the systems it was built to compare.

Benchmarks have a lifecycle. They are built, adopted, optimized against, and in time stop separating the systems they were made to compare. The saturation study from section 3 rated 29 of its 60 language model benchmarks as highly saturated, with rates rising with age. Saturation is not a failure in itself, since it can mean the capability has arrived.

According to recent reports, what a benchmark leaves behind depends on how open it was. Publishing only scores leaves future builders little they can run or adapt. When the tasks, environments, verifiers, and traces are open, each keeps working after the leaderboard stops. A solved task becomes a regression check for a newly introduced harness. Its environment and verifier can seed a harder successor. Open benchmarks also get repaired and reissued: MMLU's questions became MMLU-Redux, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 became 2.1 through community contributions. Our own walkthrough is an afterlife of this kind: raman-lab began as one task in a benchmark built for general terminal work.

That is the promise of building evaluations openly. The work that goes into an evaluation can outlive the benchmark itself, giving others a foundation to ask new questions, test new capabilities, and improve on what came before. The more we share what we build and learn, the less each new evaluation has to start from scratch.

If you’re curious what this looks like in practice, then follow our practical example.

Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. Raman spectroscopy shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the frequency of the scattered light; the resulting peaks reveal properties of the material. For graphene, an atom-thick sheet of carbon, the G and 2D peaks near 1580 and 2700 cm⁻¹ identify the number of layers. A third peak, D, appears when the lattice is disordered, and its intensity relative to G can indicate defects. Figure 5 shows the setup.

Sources indicate that figure 5. Our intended setup. A laser lights a graphene sample, and a spectrometer records how the scattered light has shifted. The agent receives that spectrum as a file, fits a curve to each peak, and saves the fitted values. The verifier checks the saved values against reference fits. The curve shown is a sketch, not measured data.

Recent findings suggest that we start by building on a task from an open benchmark. Terminal-Bench 2 already includes raman-fitting: fit a Lorentzian curve, a mathematical peak shape, to each of those two peaks and save eight parameters to /app/results.json. That gives us a runnable starting point for a narrower lab evaluation. We run these on the open source evaluation harness, Harbor. Table 2 lists what the task provides and what to check before reusing each part.

Sources indicate that table 2. What to check before reusing each component.

A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.

Recent findings suggest that for the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

It has been revealed that domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.

For your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.

Sources indicate that before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.

It has been revealed that we ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's hf-sandbox extra installed and HF_TOKEN set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.

In these commands, -t names the task, -a the agent, -e the environment, -m the model, and -k the number of rollouts per task.

The model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

In a recent development, we built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

The D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.

The original instruction.md shows why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.

In a recent development, figure 6. The instruction.md files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the fresh parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.

The verifier is guided by three rules:.

Recent findings suggest that the shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:.

Before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here datasets/my-evals contains the adapted tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.

Sources indicate that it is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in agent/trajectory.json using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.

In a recent development, the adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.

According to recent reports, figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called mark_task_complete in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.

Several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.

Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.

Finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.

The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:.

Recent findings suggest that retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.

In a recent development, A mean is more useful with its uncertainty beside it. Rollouts of the same spectrum share its difficulty, so they are not independent, and the standard error should be clustered by task. Clustering gave a mean success rate of 0.46 with a standard error of about 0.11. A repeat run passed 10 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the first run. With only eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

Harbor writes a result.json per rollout, which it calls a trial. We group these by task, check that each task has three rollouts, and record errors or exclusions. Reporting tokens, elapsed time, and tool calls beside the score lets readers compare setups that reach similar results at different costs.

Recent findings suggest that when a single model fails a task, that run alone cannot tell us what went wrong. It could be the model, the agent harness, or the evaluation itself. Running more models on the same tasks helps narrow the possibilities. When several models fail the same task, inspect the instructions, environment, and verifier for a shared cause. When one model repeatedly fails in a distinctive way, compare its traces with successful attempts.

Inference Providers serves many open-weight models through the same router, so each latest model is one more value for -m. Several providers can serve the same model with different quantization and context limits, so it helps to pin one with a suffix such as :deepinfra and record it beside the score.

Figure 8 shows the raman-lab results for each model.

According to recent reports, figure 8. raman-lab results per model, with pass@3, pass^3, and the mean pass rate with its clustered standard error. Select a square to inspect that rollout.

The comparison makes one pattern in gpt-oss-120b clearer: it often declares completion before seeing command output. In this separate run with DeepInfra pinned as the provider, it called mark_task_complete in its first response in 22 of 24 rollouts, while none of the other five models did so (Figure 9). The Step 6 run used the router's default provider and recorded 19 of 24 such early completions. It passed 11 of 24 rollouts, compared with 13 of 24 in the DeepInfra run. Both counts use the same test: whether the model called mark_task_complete in its first response.

It has been revealed that figure 9. raman-lab rollout outcomes by when the agent declared completion. Left: the agent observed command output first. Right: it called mark_task_complete in its first response.

The comparison also highlights the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Inference for all six models cost under $5 at the router's list prices. The median raman-lab rollout used about 6,000 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and about 90,000 for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. The companion repository holds the traces, the per-rollout results, and the scripts to add another model.

According to recent reports, reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. We could reuse them because Harbor and Terminal-Bench publish their code and tasks.

In a recent development, task: We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. The latest work was a narrower claim, skill coverage, and instructions for raman-lab.

Task data: The original spectrum served as a starting example. We built a generator for eight spectra with known parameters and reviewed them manually.

Environment: Harbor's environment support and HF Sandbox ran the tasks. We checked package requirements and diagnosed missing dependencies.

According to recent reports, agent harness and tools: Terminus-2 with shell access, with Inference Providers for model responses. This part needed no new work.

Rollout and trace: Harbor's rollout records and ATIF captured each run. We reviewed successes and failures and grouped them by cause.

Reference solution: We kept the convention of running solution/solve.sh and wrote a reference fit for each new task.

In a recent development, evaluation harness: Harbor ran in an HF Job. We configured the run and grouped results by task.

In a recent development, verifier: We reused the tests/test.sh entry point and its way of writing the score to a file. The new work was fit and ratio checks, plus tests for shortcuts and incorrect outputs.

It has been revealed that agent harness: The software around a model that turns its responses into actions, such as shell commands. Terminus-2 is the agent harness in this post.

Agentic evaluation: An evaluation that scores what an agent changed in an environment, not only the text it returned.

ATIF: Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, a shared format for recording an agent's messages, tool calls and observations.

Canary string: A unique marker in benchmark files that lets model trainers find and exclude them from training data.

Clustered standard error: A standard error that treats rollouts of the same task as related, which gives a wider and more honest margin than treating each rollout as independent.

Container image: A fixed package of operating system, files and software, so every rollout starts from the same environment.

Contamination: Test questions or solutions appearing in training data, so a score may reflect memory rather than skill.

Context limit: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.

D, G and 2D peaks: Features in graphene's Raman spectrum. G and 2D indicate the number of layers, and D appears when the carbon lattice has defects.

Sources indicate that defect ratio: The intensity of the D peak divided by that of the G peak, used to indicate defects in graphene. Also called the D-to-G ratio.

Development set: Tasks used while building and debugging an evaluation, as opposed to a held-back test set used for final scores.

Environment: The software, files and resources an agent works in during a task.

Evaluation harness: The software that runs tasks, repeats rollouts, collects traces and aggregates scores. Harbor is the evaluation harness in this post.

Gated dataset: A Hugging Face dataset that can be downloaded only after the owner approves an access request.

Harbor: An open-source evaluation harness for agentic tasks.

HF Job: Compute on Hugging Face that runs a script. Here it runs Harbor.

HF Sandbox: An isolated Hugging Face environment where a single rollout runs its commands and stores its files.

Held-out test set: Test items kept private so that models cannot be trained or tuned on them.

Inference Providers: A Hugging Face service that routes model requests to third-party providers through one API, called the router.

Lorentzian: A mathematical curve commonly used to model the shape of a spectral peak.

No-op agent: An agent that does nothing. A sound evaluation gives it a score of zero.

Open-weight model: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.

Oracle: An agent that runs the reference solution, used to check that every task can be solved in the supplied environment.

pass@k: The share of tasks where at least one of k rollouts succeeds.

pass^k: The share of tasks where all k rollouts succeed.

Pinning: Fixing the exact versions of software, images or model providers so a run can be repeated.

Quantization: Storing model weights at lower numerical precision to run faster and cheaper, which can change outputs slightly.

Raman shift: The difference in frequency between the laser light and the light a sample scatters, measured in cm⁻¹.

Raman spectroscopy: A technique that shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the scattered light to identify properties of the material.

Reference solution: A known correct way to complete a task, stored with the task.

Rollout: One attempt by an agent at one task. Harbor calls it a trial.

Run record: A record of what ran behind a score: the exact task, environment, model configuration and code versions.

Saturation: The point where most models reach top scores on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.

Synthetic data: Data generated from known parameters, so the correct answer is known in advance.

Terminal-Bench: An open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a computer terminal.

Recent findings suggest that terminus-2: The terminal agent harness used in this post. It connects the model to shell commands.

Token: The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.

Recent findings suggest that trace: The full record of a rollout: the model's messages, its tool calls and what each command returned. Also called a trajectory.

Verifier: The code that grades a rollout by checking the saved output or the environment's final state.

AWS Global Accelerator now preserves client IPs for NLBs with TLS listeners

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AWS Global Accelerator now preserves the client IP address for traffic sent to Network Load Balancer (NLB) endpoints with TLS listeners.
  • Previously, you couldn't add an NLB with a TLS listener to an accelerator that had client IP address preservation enabled.
  • According to recent reports, to enable this feature, add an NLB with a TLS listener as an endpoint to an accelerator with client IP address preservation setting turned on, the same way you add any NLB.

Industry observers note that AWS Global Accelerator now preserves the client IP address for traffic sent to Network Load Balancer (NLB) endpoints with TLS listeners. You can terminate TLS at your NLB and still see the original client IP address in your application. This means you can apply security groups, geo-blocking, rate limiting, fraud detection, audit logging, allowlists, and compliance controls based on the real client IP.

Previously, you couldn't add an NLB with a TLS listener to an accelerator that had client IP address preservation enabled. You had to choose between terminating TLS at the NLB and seeing the real client IP address. With this launch, you get both. This helps with workloads that need TLS termination at Layer 4, such as non-HTTP TCP protocols, applications that require static or Elastic IP addresses, and high-throughput traffic where a Layer 7 load balancer isn't a fit.

According to recent reports, to enable this feature, add an NLB with a TLS listener as an endpoint to an accelerator with client IP address preservation setting turned on, the same way you add any NLB. No additional configuration is required! Client IP address preservation for NLBs with TLS listeners is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions, excluding the AWS GovCloud (US) and China Regions. Standard Global Accelerator pricing applies.

To learn more, see Client IP address preservation in the AWS Global Accelerator Developer Guide and Create a listener for your Network Load Balancer in the User Guide for Network Load Balancers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, AWS Quick makes your legacy datasets AI ready through the fresh technology stack used by its improved visual data preparation experience.
  • When authors edit a supported legacy dataset, AWS Quick automatically opens it in the visual data preparation experience, carrying over its existing data sources, joins, transformations, and calculated fields.
  • It has been revealed that the visual data preparation experience runs on a upcoming technology stack for structured data, introduced in October 2025.

Today, AWS Quick makes your legacy datasets AI ready through the fresh technology stack used by its improved visual data preparation experience. This stack powers Dataset Semantics, topics and semantic models, and Dataset Evaluation. Data curators can add business context through dataset descriptions, column descriptions, and custom instructions. They can then compare answer accuracy before and after semantic enrichment to assess how well AI answers reflect their business definitions.

When authors edit a supported legacy dataset, AWS Quick automatically opens it in the visual data preparation experience, carrying over its existing data sources, joins, transformations, and calculated fields. Authors can then add semantics and evaluate answer accuracy without recreating the dataset.

It has been revealed that the visual data preparation experience runs on a upcoming technology stack for structured data, introduced in October 2025. It supports visual, multi-step transformations such as Append, Aggregate, and Pivot, faster ingestion for larger datasets, and up to 20 times higher cross-source join limits than the legacy experience. To make this architecture available to more legacy datasets, AWS Quick has expanded support for Google Sheets and Salesforce connectors, JODA date formats, incremental refresh, and preservation of existing unmaterialized calculated columns during legacy dataset upgrades.

This capability is available in all supported AWS Quick Regions. To learn more, see the documentation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment.

Industry observers note that A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy.

Recent findings suggest that NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing.

For simulation and training, prepare:.

Sources indicate that A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements.

Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager.

For physical-robot testing, prepare:.

A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task.

A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded.

A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles.

It has been revealed that install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies:.

Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets:.

Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically.

The environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box, office bin, bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready.

At each episode reset, the environment code automatically samples a layout, shuffles the props, and varies their placement and rotation. Most courses scatter obstacles ahead of the duck, with a smaller mix of clear paths, barriers and passages. The code also mirrors layouts and mixes aligned and staggered rows.

Sources indicate that goals start ahead of the duck. Movement commands guide it toward the goal while the policy adjusts them around obstacles.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1. Varied obstacle-course layouts with SimReady assets and primitive geometry.

Sources indicate that the IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior.

According to recent reports, during training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment.

Rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls.

It has been revealed that the obstacle-avoidance task lives in isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle. Its configuration is in obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py, ToF sensing is in sensors.py, and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under mdp/.

It has been revealed that microDuckToFCamera extends Newton’s LegacyMultiMeshRayCasterCamera to model the VL53L5CX—a compact time-of-flight (ToF) sensor on the microduck that measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz. The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck.

Real recordings informed the sensor placement and floor readings in simulation. Training adds noise, delays and missing measurements—including near the grid’s edges—to expose the policy to imperfect data. The excerpt below shows selected sensor settings already included in the task configuration. You do not need to edit or run this code separately.

Train the navigation policy with PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 training iterations. Its actor, critic, normalizers, and optimizer start fresh. The task configuration loads the fixed walking checkpoint, robot model, and obstacle assets.

The 16,384 environments shown here are configurable, not a minimum requirement. Lower --num_envs to fit your GPU’s available memory. With fewer environments collecting experience in parallel, reaching comparable policy performance may require more training iterations and longer training time. We also trained this policy on NVIDIA DGX Spark in approximately 6 hours using 4,096 parallel environments for 3,000 PPO updates, demonstrating a smaller-scale configuration for the same workflow.

Hold the stick forward to request movement; the policy adjusts the command to avoid obstacles. Release the stick to stop, press X to toggle navigation, and use Ctrl-C to end the session. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod deep health check now validates training correctness

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon SageMaker HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS now support MultiNodeTrainingValidation, a deep health check that validates nodes train correctly before your jobs run.
  • Now, The new MultiNodeTraining Validation check trains a fixed Megatron-LM workload on each instance and then across instances over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA), and fails any instance whose training loss is NaN, infinite, or diverging, or whose training doesn't finish in time.
  • MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check is available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS now support MultiNodeTrainingValidation, a deep health check that validates nodes train correctly before your jobs run. SageMaker HyperPod is purpose-built infrastructure for AI/ML model development, with built-in fault tolerance and automated cluster recovery. Previously, a GPU with a subtle fault could pass hardware stress and connectivity tests and still compute wrong results, and the first sign was often NaN or infinite loss in a production training run.

Now, The new MultiNodeTraining Validation check trains a fixed Megatron-LM workload on each instance and then across instances over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA), and fails any instance whose training loss is NaN, infinite, or diverging, or whose training doesn't finish in time. For example, you can run the check before a multi-week pre-training run, and with automatic node recovery, HyperPod reboots or replaces any instance that fails, so a faulty GPU doesn't surface days later with numerical faults in your training. You can also configure HyperPod to run the check whenever it adds instances, so new and replaced instances are validated before any jobs are scheduled on them.

MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check is available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available. To learn more about MultiNodeTrainingValidation, see deep health checks in the user guide and the blog post.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models.
  • One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture.
  • We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here.

One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs (sm100), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ.

We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint. Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs, and let it run experiments for an afternoon.

Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb.

The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script (bench.py):.

According to recent reports, bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled.

The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure:.

The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding.

In a recent development, single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate.

It has been revealed that ¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip.

All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB:.

Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work).

It has been revealed that before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job (1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s. Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits.

It has been revealed that speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s. At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth, so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer.

Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower:.

We also skipped rejection_sample_method: "fly" and "synthetic" on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup.

A few measurement complications caught us along the way:.

Before deploying, we pinned the exact vLLM nightly digest (vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6…, build 0.34.0rc1.dev1235+gf2f9edcac) and ran the acceptance gates inside a Job:.

Once those passed, we deployed the endpoint with a single hf endpoints deploy command, pinning both the image digest and model revision (authenticated access, scale-to-zero after 60 idle minutes):.

Running bench.py against the live endpoint gave 194.9 tok/s single-user, matching the Job runs once network latency is accounted for.

Everything from this run (PLAN.md, THEORY.md, jobs/driver.py, submit.sh, deploy.sh, and the raw ledger-*.jsonl files) is in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb. To reuse the loop on another model, put your candidate and control server commands into a configs/plan-*.json file and submit it to whichever HF Jobs GPU flavor matches your target endpoint.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now detects Kubernetes complications affecting training

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (249 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that amazon SageMaker HyperPod now detects Kubernetes complications that disrupt training, such as crash-looping device plugins or missing DaemonSets, on clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS.
  • Industry observers note that now, the upcoming HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches nodes, critical pods such as NVIDIA device plugins, and required DaemonSets that impact HyperPod and Kubeflow training jobs.
  • The agent is available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available and you can install it with a helm chart.

Recent findings suggest that amazon SageMaker HyperPod now detects Kubernetes complications that disrupt training, such as crash-looping device plugins or missing DaemonSets, on clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS. SageMaker HyperPod is purpose-built infrastructure for AI/ML model development, with built-in fault tolerance and automated cluster recovery. Previously, when a device plugin crash-looped or a taint evicted a job's pods, the job's error rarely named the pod or node, so engineers pieced the cause together from kubectl output and per-rank logs.

Industry observers note that now, the upcoming HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches nodes, critical pods such as NVIDIA device plugins, and required DaemonSets that impact HyperPod and Kubeflow training jobs. The agent correlates Kubernetes concerns with the training jobs they affect and reports them as Kubernetes events and Amazon CloudWatch logs. For example, if a device plugin keeps crashing on one node mid training run, the agent flags the node as it loses GPUs and, when the job fails, logs the failure reason with the pods and nodes involved, so you can fix that node and restart sooner. For jobs that opt in, it also highlights which rank fell behind when NCCL communication stalls, while the job is still running.

The agent is available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available and you can install it with a helm chart. To learn more, see Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent in the user guide and the blog post.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

Sources indicate that we built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:.

If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

In a recent development, CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:.

The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

It has been revealed that adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:.

Industry observers note that you do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:.

In a recent development, want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

Industry observers note that this approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

#34035. Tech Report: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1659 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished.
  • These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science.
  • Industry observers note that to better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

Industry observers note that to better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

Sources indicate that one of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.

Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”.

Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

Industry observers note that participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher remarked.

Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

It has been revealed that the same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Meanwhile, participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used.

Recent findings suggest that both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

It has been revealed that this is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

In a recent development, researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

Sources indicate that it will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify vital concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

It has been revealed that still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

The promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.

If you used the ParkMobile app to pay for parking at a meter several years ago, you might be getting a payment as a result of a data breach. Unfortunately, it’s probably not an amount you’d expect for the inconvenience of having your data exposed. And while it’s a comically low amount, don’t spend it all in one place, because, well…. You’re literally not allowed to.

Here’s what’s happening and why the ParkMobile data beach settlement is raising eyebrows online.

Also: Hackers stole 1 billion records from Salesforce customer databases with this simple trick – don’t fall for it.

Recent findings suggest that in 2021, hackers accessed sensitive data from more than 21 million ParkMobile customers, including license plate numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, and mailing addresses. The hackers didn’t get any payment information.

ParkMobile denied any wrongdoing but agreed to a settlement to avoid the cost and time of going to court. If you filed a claim, you could choose to get your payment in cash — up to $25. If you didn’t file a claim but you were still affected, you probably received an email this week with your alternative payment — $1.

“As part of the agreed resolution,” the email explained, “you are entitled to receive a benefit.” The email went on to say that the benefit is a $1 discount code for the ParkMobile app.

First, the payment is only good for credit towards ParkMobile service fees (not even the actual parking fee), so you have to park at a ParkMobile-owned lot to use your benefit. Second, you have to enter the code you received manually in your account. Third, you can’t use your $1 all at once.

Industry observers note that your code is good for 25 cents off a ParkMobile service fee, the email explained, and it can be used up to four times, equaling $1. When I searched a few ParkMobile lots near me, service fees were between $1.80 and $4.

Get the biggest stories in tech every Friday with ZDNET’s Week in Review newsletter.

Naturally, users who received the email were quick to criticize. Several Reddit posts appeared, with users pointing out that you had to pay significantly more than your benefit to actually use it, claiming the settlement was just a ploy for lawyers to get paid, and some saying they thought the email was a phishing attempt.

Customers who received a $1 code have one year to use it.
